For a student with extensive support needs, ordinary moments often make the strongest starting points: arriving, communicating a refusal, waiting for lunch, joining a shared activity, using the bathroom privately, or leaving with the right equipment. Describe the support involved, not just whether an activity was completed. An illustrative note might read: “At home, choices are easier when two objects are offered with time to respond. What choice-making opportunities are available during the school day?” This invites comparison without pretending a home observation answers every school question. Include something the student enjoys and how they show interest. Use age-respectful language. A teenager who needs hands-on assistance is still a teenager, with a developing history, relationships, and preferences. Keep other concerns on a second page so you do not have to carry them in your head. Prioritizing is an organizing choice; it does not mean other needs cease to matter. For each priority, collect one or two relevant items: A dated observation or communication from schoolThe related IEP section or goalA recent progress report or assessment findingA short question about information that is missing You do not need to prove a complete case before asking a question. “I cannot tell from this report how much help was needed” is a useful observation. Ask who can explain the information and what additional information would help the Team decide. Under federal IDEA, an IEP Team must consider the student's strengths, parent concerns, evaluation results, and academic, developmental, and functional needs. That is a reason to bring your observations into the discussion, without assuming that every requested service will necessarily be adopted. Read the federal IEP-development rule. Sitting three: make the meeting easier to use+Confirm the date, expected length, participants, and how you will join. Request the documents you need and any access arrangements, such as interpretation or readable electronic copies. Send your short agenda ahead when possible and keep a copy in front of you. Massachusetts note: upon request, assessment summaries must be available to parents at least two days before the relevant Team discussion under 603 CMR 28.04(2)(c). This provision is specifically about assessment summaries; it is not a universal two-day deadline for all meeting papers. Ask early and identify the reports you need. Read the Massachusetts evaluation regulation. Prepare two sentences you can return to: “Today I would like us to understand [need] and discuss [request]. Before we finish, could we review the next steps and who is responsible for each?” This is an example script to adapt privately. It is fine to read it aloud. Leave space for the unexpected+Put a blank page beside your agenda. If new information arrives, write the document name, the question it raises, and whether you need time to review it. Ask for plain-language explanations. You can say, “I need a moment to understand that,” or, “Could we return to the question about support during transitions?” When energy is very limited, use the smallest version: one priority, one supporting observation, one question. That is meaningful preparation. Your knowledge of the student's daily life belongs in the room whether you arrive with three pages or three sentences. It made the room feel a little more human before we started. Now everyone appears in a tiny square. How do we begin without feeling awkward?” This is an editorial example, not a submitted letter. The feeling behind it is familiar: the small rituals around a meeting can help people settle in, and a video call sometimes removes all of them. Keep the welcome small and genuine+You can preserve the spirit of that gesture with a short hello, an accurate thank-you, or a brief observation about the student. You do not need to replace muffins with mailed gifts, an elaborate presentation, or a performance of cheerfulness. Try: “Good morning. Thank you for making the time. We appreciated receiving the report in advance. I have three questions I would like us to work through today.” Only use the thank-you if it is true. If the past week has been difficult, a simple “Thank you for joining” is enough. Parents do not have to be charming to participate meaningfully, and access to appropriate education should never depend on refreshments or social ease. Warmth and a firm request can occupy the same sentence: “I appreciate the work that went into this. I still need us to address how the plan will work during lunch.” Give the first two minutes a little structure+Ask for names and roles, particularly when someone has joined by phone or is using a shared device. Confirm when the meeting is expected to end and whether anyone needs to leave early. Then explain what you hope to cover. An example opening: “Before we start, could everyone introduce themselves and their role? I would like to begin with a short update about what is working, then discuss communication access and transitions. Could we leave a few minutes at the end to confirm decisions and next steps?” That final sentence makes a request about how to use the time. It does not promise that every question will be resolved in one sitting. If the agenda is too full, ask which items will be addressed now and how the remaining discussion will happen. Make your own small meeting station+Set out the same things you would want at a physical table: your agenda, the current IEP, a pen, water, and a place to write unfamiliar terms. Close unrelated tabs before sharing your screen. Keep the meeting link and a contact number where you can find them if the connection drops. You can ask for a dial-in option, a technology check, captions, interpretation, or another arrangement that would help you participate. Explain the barrier rather than assuming the school knows it. Under federal IDEA, parents and the public agency may agree to video or conference-call participation. Read the alternative-participation rule. The school also has responsibilities to support parent participation, including scheduling at a mutually agreed time and place. A virtual invitation alone does not solve every participation problem. Read the parent-participation rule. Have a graceful interruption ready+Video calls make it harder to notice when somebody is trying to speak. Choose a plain phrase you can use without apologizing repeatedly: “I have a question before we move to the next section.”“The audio cut out. Please repeat the proposed change.”“Could you put that document on screen and identify the section?”“I am hearing two different descriptions. Could we clarify which is correct?” If you need a pause, ask for one. If you are upset, you can name the practical need: “I need five minutes, then I would like to continue with this question.” At the close, thank people for a specific helpful action if you wish, then confirm what remains open. The most useful replacement for the muffin ritual may be very ordinary: a welcome, a readable agenda, and enough room for everyone to understand what happens next. Federal IDEA includes parents as IEP Team members and requires consideration of parent concerns in developing the IEP. Bringing an agenda is one practical way to organize that contribution. Copy this working template+Use the prompts below in a document you keep privately. Replace the brackets before sharing it with the appropriate school team. Make each request easy to recognize+“Communication” is a subject. “Can we review how the student can make a choice during arrival, class activities, lunch, and dismissal?” gives the Team something concrete to answer. Likewise, “More data” can become: “Please explain what was counted, during which activities, and with what level of assistance.” You are asking to understand the information, rather than assuming that a percentage has a single obvious meaning. Separate your observation from your interpretation. “The report lists three opportunities” is an observation. “There may be too few opportunities to practice” is a question to explore. Both can belong on the page when the distinction is clear. Use the page during the conversation+Send the agenda ahead if that is practical. If someone offers an answer that you do not understand, write a question mark rather than pretending it is settled. If time runs short, read the remaining requests aloud and ask how they will be handled. Avoid packing a major concern into an unexplained last-minute attachment. Afterward, use your marked agenda to prepare a short follow-up note. Save the original and your notes separately so you can tell what you planned to ask from what you actually heard. Its Massachusetts guide also notes that there is no formal certification or licensing process for advocates and that most are not trained as lawyers. A course certificate should therefore be understood in context, rather than treated as proof of government licensure or legal authority. Read FCSN's advocate-selection guidance. Ask what a credential means, who issued it, what training or assessment was involved, and whether any separate professional license is being claimed. Check a claimed license with the relevant licensing body. Requirements and permitted activities can differ by location; get local advice about legal representation. Compare three areas of fit+Experience with the work you need Ask: “What experience do you have helping families with needs similar to ours, and what would you want to learn before suggesting a plan?” A useful answer explains a process and acknowledges the limits of what can be known during an introductory call. You can also ask which school systems or settings they know, how they stay current, and whether they have relationships that could create a conflict of interest. Experience with a district may be helpful, but a personal connection is no guarantee of an outcome. How you will work together Try these questions: How do you include the student's preferences and communication?How do you distinguish observations, educational recommendations, and legal questions?May I review emails or documents before you send them on my behalf?What happens when you and I disagree about an approach?When would you recommend consulting an attorney or another specialist? Ask for an anonymized description of their process, not another family's private records. References, when available and appropriately authorized, can help you learn whether the advocate communicates clearly and follows through. What the work will cost Request a written explanation of the rate, billing increments, minimum charges, and any retainer. Ask whether reviewing files, travel, preparation, phone calls, brief emails, cancellations, and post-meeting notes are billable. Clarify who does the work and whether different staff have different rates. Then describe a bounded first task: “Please estimate the time and cost to review these documents and have one preparation call. Contact me before going beyond that scope.” An estimate may change when more information emerges; agree in advance on how changes will be approved. Use a simple comparison card+For each person, record: Relevant experience and any independently verified credentialsFirst task they propose and the reason for itWhat they will deliver, and whenEstimated cost and possible additional chargesCommunication expectations and your control over outgoing messagesConflicts, confidentiality practices, and how the relationship can endQuestions still unanswered You do not need a numerical score. “Explains clearly,” “uncertain about costs,” and “needs follow-up” may tell you more than a five-star rating. Notice promises that deserve a second look+Be cautious with guaranteed placements, promises that a particular phrase will force a result, pressure to sign immediately, or advice to exaggerate. A careful advocate can be direct about a concern while remaining honest about uncertainty and the limits of their role. Before paying, ask about available parent information and training. In Massachusetts, FCSN's special education resources are a useful starting point. Ask the organization about current support options, eligibility, and any charges rather than assuming all services or referrals are free. The goal of an introductory conversation is a comprehensible next step. You should leave knowing what help is proposed, what it costs, and which decisions remain yours.
